readNotes: Pilot batch 2 (Nov 4 2026). Full text read first. Ledger reuse allowed for reader items (Brandon, Nov 4 3:58 PM). Distractors from chapters 0-6 only; sexual passages avoided.

v1.text: Just as a potter's wheel, once it has been set in motion, will keep on turning for a long time and only slowly lose its vigour and come to a stop, thus Siddhartha's soul had kept on turning the wheel of asceticism, the wheel of thinking, the wheel of differentiation for a long time, still turning, but it turned slowly and hesitantly and was close to coming to a standstill. Slowly, like humidity entering the dying stem of a tree, filling it slowly and making it rot, the world and sloth had entered Siddhartha's soul, slowly it filled his soul, made it heavy, made it tired, put it to sleep.

v2.text: But still he had felt different from and superior to the others; always he had watched them with some mockery, some mocking disdain, with the same disdain which a Samana constantly feels for the people of the world. When Kamaswami was ailing, when he was annoyed, when he felt insulted, when he was vexed by his worries as a merchant, Siddhartha had always watched it with mockery. Just slowly and imperceptibly, as the harvest seasons and rainy seasons passed by, his mockery had become more tired, his superiority had become more quiet.

v3.text: And yet, he envied them, envied them just the more, the more similar he became to them. He envied them for the one thing that was missing from him and that they had, the importance they were able to attach to their lives, the amount of passion in their joys and fears, the fearful but sweet happiness of being constantly in love. These people were all of the time in love with themselves, with women, with their children, with honours or money, with plans or hopes.

v4.text: Like a veil, like a thin mist, tiredness came over Siddhartha, slowly, getting a bit denser every day, a bit murkier every month, a bit heavier every year. As a new dress becomes old in time, loses its beautiful colour in time, gets stains, gets wrinkles, gets worn off at the seams, and starts to show threadbare spots here and there, thus Siddhartha's new life, which he had started after his separation from Govinda, had grown old, lost colour and splendour as the years passed by, was gathering wrinkles and stains, and hidden at bottom, already showing its ugliness here and there, disappointment and disgust were waiting. Siddhartha did not notice it. He only noticed that this bright and reliable voice inside of him, which had awoken in him at that time and had ever guided him in his best times, had become silent.

v5.text: Thus he gambled with high stakes and mercilessly, hating himself, mocking himself, won thousands, threw away thousands, lost money, lost jewelry, lost a house in the country, won again, lost again. That fear, that terrible and petrifying fear, which he felt while he was rolling the dice, while he was worried about losing high stakes, that fear he loved and sought to always renew it, always increase it, always get it to a slightly higher level, for in this feeling alone he still felt something like happiness, something like an intoxication, something like an elevated form of life in the midst of his saturated, lukewarm, dull life.

v6.text: He, who gambled away tens of thousands at one roll of the dice and laughed at it, became more strict and more petty in his business, occasionally dreaming at night about money! And whenever he woke up from this ugly spell, whenever he found his face in the mirror at the bedroom's wall to have aged and become more ugly, whenever embarrassment and disgust came over him, he continued fleeing, fleeing into a new game, fleeing into a numbing of his mind brought on by sex, by wine, and from there he fled back into the urge to pile up and obtain possessions. In this pointless cycle he ran, growing tired, growing old, growing ill.

v7.text: Kamala owned a small, rare singing bird in a golden cage. Of this bird he dreamt. He dreamt: this bird had become mute, who at other times always used to sing in the morning, and since this arose his attention, he stepped in front of the cage and looked inside; there the small bird was dead and lay stiff on the ground. He took it out, weighed it for a moment in his hand, and then threw it away, out in the street, and in the same moment, he felt terribly shocked, and his heart hurt, as if he had thrown away from himself all value and everything good by throwing out this dead bird.

v8.text: Starting up from this dream, he felt encompassed by a deep sadness. Worthless, so it seemed to him, worthless and pointless was the way he had been going through life; nothing which was alive, nothing which was in some way delicious or worth keeping he had left in his hands. Alone he stood there and empty like a castaway on the shore.

v9.text: For how long had he not heard this voice any more, for how long had he reached no height any more, how even and dull was the manner in which his path had passed through life, for many long years, without a high goal, without thirst, without elevation, content with small lustful pleasures and yet never satisfied! For all of these many years, without knowing it himself, he had tried hard and longed to become a man like those many, like those children, and in all this, his life had been much more miserable and poorer than theirs, and their goals were not his, nor their worries; after all, that entire world of the Kamaswami-people had only been a game to him, a dance he would watch, a comedy.

v10.text: Only Kamala had been dear, had been valuable to him—but was she still thus? Did he still need her, or she him? Did they not play a game without an ending? Was it necessary to live for this? No, it was not necessary! The name of this game was Sansara, a game for children, a game which was perhaps enjoyable to play once, twice, ten times—but for ever and ever over again?

v11.text: In the same hour of the night, Siddhartha left his garden, left the city, and never came back. For a long time, Kamaswami had people look for him, thinking that he had fallen into the hands of robbers. Kamala had no one look for him. When she was told that Siddhartha had disappeared, she was not astonished. Did she not always expect it? Was he not a Samana, a man who was at home nowhere, a pilgrim?

v12.text: When she received the first news of Siddhartha's disappearance, she went to the window, where she held a rare singing bird captive in a golden cage. She opened the door of the cage, took the bird out and let it fly. For a long time, she gazed after it, the flying bird. From this day on, she received no more visitors and kept her house locked.

v13.text: And after each big loss, his mind was set on new riches, pursued the trade more zealously, forced his debtors more strictly to pay, because he wanted to continue gambling, he wanted to continue squandering, continue demonstrating his disdain of wealth. Siddhartha lost his calmness when losses occurred, lost his patience when he was not paid on time, lost his kindness towards beggars, lost his disposition for giving away and loaning money to those who petitioned him.

A.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the passage?
options: Siddhartha decides to buy a new songbird for Kamala.
After the dream, Siddhartha feels proud of all the riches he has gathered in the city.
After the dream, Siddhartha feels his whole way of life has been worthless.
Siddhartha dreams of a ship far out at sea.
A.explanation: He feels "worthless and pointless was the way he had been going through life." Pride in riches is the opposite. The castaway on the shore is a comparison, not a dream of a ship. No new bird is mentioned. The dead songbird stands for the inner life he has let die in the city.

A.prompt: According to the passage, what did Siddhartha do with the dead bird in his dream?
options: He buried it under the mango tree and wept.
He threw it out into the street.
He put it back into its golden cage.
He gave it back to Kamala.
A.explanation: He "threw it away, out in the street." He does not bury it or weep beside a grave. He does not give it to Kamala. He takes it out of the cage and weighs it, then throws it away rather than returning it.

A.prompt: As used in the passage, "envied" most nearly means
options: taught
pitied
was jealous of
looked down on
A.explanation: He "envied them for the one thing that was missing from him," so he was jealous of what they had. Looking down with disdain is his earlier attitude, which the passage turns from with "And yet." Pity and teaching do not fit wanting what others have.

A.prompt: Kamala's act of letting the bird fly suggests that she
options: wants to buy a different, livelier bird
plans to follow the bird into the forest to bring Siddhartha back
is angry with the bird for not singing
is letting go of what she has held captive
A.explanation: She opens the cage and lets the bird go on hearing that Siddhartha has gone, suggesting she lets go. She does not follow; she locks her house. No new bird is mentioned. She gazes after it a long time, which suggests feeling, not anger.

A.prompt: Based on the passage, how did Kamala react when told that Siddhartha had disappeared?
options: She was not surprised.
She fainted from shock.
She laughed at the news.
She sent people to search the roads.
A.explanation: The passage says "she was not astonished." Kamaswami, not Kamala, "had people look for him, thinking that he had fallen into the hands of robbers." She does not laugh or faint; she reflects that she "always" expected it. Her calm response shows she had long expected him to leave one day.

A.prompt: Which choice provides the best evidence for the answer to the previous question?
options: "In the same hour of the night, Siddhartha left his garden"
"Kamaswami had people look for him, thinking that he had fallen into the hands of robbers."
"When she was told that Siddhartha had disappeared, she was not astonished."
"Kamala had no one look for him."
A.explanation: Only "she was not astonished" states her reaction. The Kamaswami line describes his reaction, not hers. "Siddhartha left his garden" describes his departure. "Had no one look for him" shows what she did not do, but not directly that she was unsurprised.

A.prompt: The repetition of "fleeing" mainly serves to
options: describe Siddhartha running from robbers at night
explain the rules of the game of dice
show how fast and far he can run
show Siddhartha running in a pointless cycle
A.explanation: He keeps "fleeing into a new game, fleeing into a numbing," then back to possessions: "In this pointless cycle he ran." No robbers chase him. It is not about physical speed. The rules of dice are not explained. The repeated word shows a man trapped in a cycle he cannot escape.

A.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the passage?
options: Siddhartha's mockery of others slowly faded as he became more like them.
Siddhartha left the city in anger after a quarrel.
Kamaswami slowly learned to mock Siddhartha and his strange Samana ways.
Siddhartha grew more proud and mocking with every year in the city.
A.explanation: "Slowly and imperceptibly... his mockery had become more tired," and he took on something of the childlike people's ways. Growing more mocking reverses this. Kamaswami is mocked, not mocking. Leaving the city is not in this passage. The passage traces a slow loss of distance until he has become like the people he once mocked.

A.prompt: According to the passage, what did Kamala do from that day on?
options: She received no more visitors and kept her house locked.
She opened her house to every pilgrim passing through.
She sold her pleasure-garden to Kamaswami.
She went to live in the forest.
A.explanation: The passage says "she received no more visitors and kept her house locked." Opening her house reverses this. Going to the forest and selling the garden are not mentioned in this passage. Her closed house shows that she, too, is withdrawing from her old life after he leaves her.

A.prompt: As used in the passage, "castaway" most nearly means
options: a sailor on watch
a fisherman far at sea
a merchant
a shipwrecked person
A.explanation: He stood "alone... and empty like a castaway on the shore," so it means a shipwrecked person left alone. A fisherman with a catch suggests plenty, not emptiness. A merchant and a sailor on watch lack the sense of being stranded alone.

A.prompt: Siddhartha's questions suggest that he now finds the life he has been living
options: full of high goals and purpose
pointless when repeated without end
too short to enjoy
more exciting than ever before, game after game
A.explanation: He calls it "a game for children," enjoyable "once, twice, ten times—but for ever and ever over again?" so endless repetition seems pointless. He is not excited. Its length is the problem, not shortness. He has no high goals here.

A.prompt: The comparison "Like a veil, like a thin mist" suggests that Siddhartha's tiredness
options: made him see more clearly than before
came over him gradually and almost unseen
was easy to brush away
struck him suddenly like a heavy blow
A.explanation: A veil and mist settle softly, and the tiredness came "slowly, getting a bit denser every day," so it came gradually. A sudden blow is the opposite. Mist blurs rather than clears vision. "Siddhartha did not notice it," so it was not easy to see or remove.

B.prompt: According to the passage, what feeling did Siddhartha love while gambling?
options: The fear he felt while rolling the dice
Joy in the company of his friends
Pride in his skill at dice
The calm he felt when he won large sums
B.explanation: The passage says "that fear, that terrible and petrifying fear... that fear he loved and sought to always renew." Calm is not what he loved. Pride and friendship are not named; he found in fear "something like happiness." He loved this fear because it was the only strong feeling left in his empty life.

B.prompt: As used in the passage, "vigour" most nearly means
options: direction
energy
weight
colour
B.explanation: A potter's wheel will "slowly lose its vigour and come to a stop," so vigour means energy of motion. Direction is not lost; speed is. Colour and weight do not change as a wheel slows. The word describes the force that drives his life onward, like a potter's wheel turning.

B.prompt: The passage suggests that Siddhartha envies the childlike people mainly for
options: their wisdom
their wealth, far larger than his own
the passion they bring to their lives
their freedom from love and its pains
B.explanation: He envied "the importance they were able to attach to their lives, the amount of passion in their joys and fears." He is rich himself. He does not call them wise. They are "all of the time in love," so freedom from love is wrong.

B.prompt: How does Siddhartha now judge his many years in the city?
options: As years without a high goal or true satisfaction
As years spent studying the merchant's books
As years of fasting and waiting
As the happiest and most meaningful years of his life
B.explanation: He sees a path "without a high goal, without thirst, without elevation... and yet never satisfied!" "The happiest and most meaningful years" reverses this. He did not study or fast in the city; he sought "small lustful pleasures." His judgment shows that the comforts of the city never gave him a real purpose.

B.prompt: Which choice provides the best evidence for the answer to the previous question?
options: "For all of these many years, without knowing it himself"
"after all, that entire world of the Kamaswami-people had only been a game to him"
"For how long had he not heard this voice any more"
"without a high goal, without thirst, without elevation, content with small lustful pleasures and yet never satisfied!"
B.explanation: Only the "without a high goal" line gives his judgment of those years. "For how long had he not heard this voice" notes the loss of the voice. The "only been a game" line describes his detachment. "Without knowing it himself" introduces the next thought but contains no judgment.

B.prompt: The comparison to a new dress that "becomes old in time" mainly serves to
options: explain his trade in cloth and silk
describe the stained clothes he wears to Kamala's garden
show how his new life aged step by step
show that he likes fine and costly clothes
B.explanation: Like a dress that "loses its beautiful colour... gets stains, gets wrinkles," his "new life... had grown old." The dress is a comparison, not his actual clothing. It is not about liking clothes. Trade in cloth is not mentioned. The image of a dress growing old shows decay that happens slowly and almost unseen.

B.prompt: Which choice best states the central idea of the passage?
options: Gambling drove Siddhartha into pettiness, greed and a pointless cycle.
Siddhartha learned from his losses and became more generous to debtors.
Siddhartha gave all his money to Kamala.
Siddhartha stopped gambling after one great loss.
B.explanation: He "became more strict and more petty," fled back "into the urge to pile up and obtain possessions," and ran "in this pointless cycle." Becoming generous to debtors reverses his growing pettiness. He kept gambling. Giving money to Kamala is not mentioned.

B.prompt: As used in the passage, "imperceptibly" most nearly means
options: unwillingly
quickly
unnoticeably
loudly
B.explanation: "Just slowly and imperceptibly... his mockery had become more tired," so the change happened unnoticeably. Loudly contradicts the quiet change. "Unwillingly" adds a feeling not stated. "Quickly" contradicts "slowly." The change happened so gradually that Siddhartha himself hardly noticed it taking place in him day by day.

B.prompt: The phrase "and in the same moment, he felt terribly shocked" mainly serves to
options: introduce Kamala into the dream
show that the bird came back to life and flew off
describe the stormy weather that night
mark the turn from a careless act to sudden grief
B.explanation: He casually throws the bird away, then "in the same moment" feels shocked, as if he had "thrown away... all value," turning the scene. The bird is dead and does not revive. Kamala does not appear. No weather is described.

B.prompt: The passage suggests that Siddhartha's spiritual habits continued mainly because
options: Kamala encouraged them
they kept moving for a time from earlier force
he worked hard each day to practise them more carefully
Kamaswami required them of his partner
B.explanation: Like a wheel "once it has been set in motion," his soul "kept on turning... for a long time," continuing from earlier force. He did not practise harder; the wheel "turned slowly." Kamala and Kamaswami are not mentioned in this passage.

B.prompt: The questions near the end of the passage mainly present
options: Siddhartha's own regret
the robbers' plans for him
Kamaswami's complaints about losing his partner and his money
Kamala's view of why she expected Siddhartha to leave
B.explanation: "Did she not always expect it? Was he not a Samana... a pilgrim?" give Kamala's thoughts. Kamaswami searched but does not complain here. Siddhartha has left; these are not his thoughts. Robbers appear only in Kamaswami's guess. Her questions show that she understood him better than Kamaswami ever did.

B.prompt: How does the bird in Passage 2 relate to the bird in Passage 1?
options: Passage 2 shows the bird singing sweetly to Kamala.
Both bird scenes mark something precious being let go.
Passage 2 shows Siddhartha buying the bird.
In both passages the bird dies and is thrown away.
B.explanation: In the dream he throws away the dead bird and feels he lost "all value"; Kamala lets the living bird fly when Siddhartha leaves. The bird in Passage 2 is alive and set free. Siddhartha buys nothing. The bird flies away rather than sings.

C.prompt: Which choice best states the central idea of the passage?
options: He bought a new dress for Kamala.
He noticed his tiredness at once.
His new life grew brighter each year as his inner voice spoke more clearly.
His new life slowly grew old as his inner voice fell silent.
C.explanation: His new life "had grown old, lost colour," and "this bright and reliable voice... had become silent." The second choice reverses both points. The dress is a comparison. "Siddhartha did not notice it," so he did not notice at once.

C.prompt: The passage suggests that Siddhartha gambled partly to
options: grow richer than Kamaswami and leave his business
feel alive through fear, even while hating himself
pass the time calmly
please Kamala
C.explanation: He gambled "hating himself, mocking himself," and in the fear of losing he "felt something like happiness... an elevated form of life." Growing richer is not his aim; he "threw away thousands" and "lost a house in the country." Kamala is not mentioned. He gambles "mercilessly" and with fear, not to pass the time calmly.

C.prompt: The series of phrases beginning with "without" mainly serves to
options: stress the emptiness of his years in the city
show that he had no money left
describe the poor people of the city
list the things he gave up as a young Samana
C.explanation: "Without a high goal, without thirst, without elevation" stresses the emptiness of his recent years. It does not describe his Samana youth. The poor are not described. He was rich; the lack is spiritual, not money. The repeated word "without" piles up everything his years in the city have lacked.

C.prompt: What happened to Siddhartha's spiritual habits over time?
options: They stopped all at once.
They never changed in any way.
They slowed and came close to stopping.
They grew stronger each year, as in the forest.
C.explanation: His soul's wheel "turned slowly and hesitantly and was close to coming to a standstill." The second choice reverses the slowing. "Slowly lose its vigour" rules out stopping at once. They clearly changed. The habits slowed like a wheel losing the push that first set it spinning.

C.prompt: Which choice provides the best evidence for the answer to the previous question?
options: "Just as a potter's wheel, once it has been set in motion, will keep on turning for a long time"
"thus Siddhartha's soul had kept on turning the wheel of asceticism, the wheel of thinking"
"but it turned slowly and hesitantly and was close to coming to a standstill."
"made it heavy, made it tired, put it to sleep."
C.explanation: Only the "close to coming to a standstill" line states what happened to his habits. The potter's wheel line sets up the comparison. The "kept on turning" line says the habits continued, not that they slowed. "Put it to sleep" describes his soul, not specifically the wheel of practice.

C.prompt: As used in the passage, "squandering" most nearly means
options: saving
lending
counting
wasting
C.explanation: He "wanted to continue squandering" money at dice, so it means wasting. Saving is the opposite. "Counting" and "lending" are business actions, but he squanders to show "disdain of wealth." After each big loss he pursued new riches only so that he could go on gambling and throwing money away.

C.prompt: The comparison "like humidity entering the dying stem of a tree" suggests that the world entered his soul
options: without any effect at all
to make it stronger
quickly, like a sudden storm
slowly, causing hidden decay
C.explanation: Humidity fills the stem "slowly and making it rot," so the world entered gradually and caused decay. A sudden storm contradicts "slowly." Rot weakens rather than strengthens. It "made it heavy, made it tired," so it had an effect. The image of rot spreading inside a dying stem fits the slow decay of his soul.

C.prompt: The passage suggests that treating the city as had "only been a game" left Siddhartha
options: richer in spirit than all the merchants he knew
poorer in life than the people he watched
a better and richer merchant
free of all his worries
C.explanation: "His life had been much more miserable and poorer than theirs," since their world was only "a comedy" to him. He is not richer in spirit. He was not free; he was "never satisfied." Business skill is not the point here.

C.prompt: The list "with women, with their children, with honours or money, with plans or hopes" mainly serves to
options: show the many things the childlike people love
name the things Siddhartha has always despised
list Kamala's many visitors
describe a busy market
C.explanation: The people "were all of the time in love with themselves, with women, with their children..." so the list shows how much they love. Siddhartha envies, not despises, this. Kamala's visitors are not listed. No market is described. The list shows the things that give the childlike people their passion for life.

C.prompt: The series of questions in the passage mainly presents
options: Kamaswami's worries about business
Siddhartha's inner reckoning with his life
a lesson remembered from Gotama
a conversation in which Kamala asks him to stay
C.explanation: "Did he still need her, or she him?... Was it necessary to live for this?" are his own questions, answered "No." Kamala does not speak. Kamaswami is not present. Gotama gives no lesson here. The questions are his own inner reckoning after the dream about the dead bird.

C.prompt: How does Passage 2 develop the change begun in Passage 1?
options: It shows Siddhartha recovering his old superiority and mocking people again.
It shows Siddhartha leaving the city.
It shows the slow change turning into greed and pettiness.
It shows Kamaswami becoming generous.
C.explanation: Passage 1 shows mockery fading as he becomes like others; Passage 2 shows him "more strict and more petty," piling up possessions. He does not recover superiority. He has not yet left. Kamaswami is not shown changing. The second passage shows the earlier slow change ending in petty greed and anger.

C.prompt: How does Passage 2 build on the feeling in Passage 1?
options: It turns his sense of worthlessness into a judgment that the game must end.
It shows him deciding his life has been worthwhile and should go on.
It shows Kamala comforting him in her garden.
It describes another dream about the bird.
C.explanation: Passage 1 calls his life "worthless and pointless"; Passage 2 asks "Was it necessary to live for this? No," judging the game should end. He does not decide to go on. No new dream is told. Kamala is not present.
